title: Sounds & spelling
subtitle: Long and short vowels, tricky letter pairs and how to read Dutch words

explain.text: Dutch spelling is quite regular once you know one rule. A vowel can be **short** or **long**, and the spelling shows which. A long vowel in a closed syllable (one that ends in a consonant) is written with **two letters**: *maan*, *boot*, *veer*, *buur*. A short vowel is written with **one letter**: *man*, *bot*, *ver*, *bus*.

explain.nl: De man kijkt naar de maan.
explain.en: The man looks at the moon.

explain.text: When you add an ending, the syllable can open up. *maan* becomes *manen* (ma-nen): the long vowel now stands alone in an open syllable, so one letter is enough. A short vowel stays short, so the consonant is doubled: *man → mannen* (man-nen).
Short vowel + double consonant (*mannen*), long vowel + single consonant (*manen*). This pattern comes back in plurals and verbs.

explain.nl: Twee mannen lopen onder de maan.
explain.en: Two men walk under the moon.

lessons.title: Letter pairs: ui, ij, au, eu, oe

explain.text: Some vowel pairs make one sound. Say them out loud: **ui** (*huis, uit*), **ij** and **ei** (both close to the *ay* in *day*, but more open: *prijs, trein*), **au** and **ou** (the same sound: *blauw, koud*), **eu** (*leuk, neus*), **oe** (like *oo* in *food*: *boek, goed*) and **ie** (like *ee* in *see*: *fiets, bier*).

explain.text: *ij* and *ei* sound the same, and so do *au* and *ou*. You have to learn which spelling a word uses: *tijd* and *prijs* with *ij*, but *trein* and *ei* with *ei*. Both spelling pairs are in the dictionary, so check the word when you are not sure.

explain.text: Dutch **g** and **ch** are both a scratchy sound at the back of the throat, a bit like clearing your throat softly: *goed, groot, nacht, lachen*. (In the south of the country the *g* is softer.) In *sch-* at the start of a word you hear **s + ch**: *school, schrijven, schaap*.

explain.en: I am going to school today.

explain.text: Two endings are worth learning early. **-ig** is pronounced with a very weak vowel, a bit like *-ugh*: *koning, vijftig, gezellig*. **-lijk** sounds like *-luk*: *natuurlijk, mogelijk, vriendelijk*. The vowel in these endings is short and weak, so don't stress it.

explain.text: The letter *e* at the end of a word, and in *de*, *het*, *een*, is a weak 'uh' sound (like the *a* in *about*). Don't say it as 'ay'.

explain.en: Of course it is very cosy.
